extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners preparing/responding to Office actions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, applying, and rebutting rejections under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 (anticipation, public use/sale, inventorship, foreign patenting, and obviousness), including provisional rejections, disqualification under 103(c), and requirements for continuing-application benefit claims under 35 U.S.C. 120.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (required elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: After indicating that the rejection is under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth in the Office action: (A) the relevant teachings of the prior art relied upon, preferably with reference to the relevant column or page number(s) and line number(s) where appropriate; (B) the difference or differences in the claim over the applied reference(s); (C) the proposed modification of the applied reference(s) necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; and (D) an explanation why one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made would have been motivated to make the proposed modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific citations to the prior art (columns/pages/lines) where appropriate. Explicitly state claim/reference differences and the exact modification(s) hypothesized. Explain the motivation to combine/modify in clear factual/legal terms so issues are identifiable early and the applicant can fairly reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness, three basic criteria must be met: (1) some suggestion or motivation, either in the references themselves or in the general knowledge available to one of ordinary skill, to modify or combine reference teachings; (2) a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) the prior art reference(s) must teach or suggest all claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teaching/suggestion to make the claimed combination and the reasonable expectation of success must both be found in the prior art and not based on applicant’s disclosure. See MPEP §§ 2141–2144.09 for decisions and examples. Examiner must support each prong in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner burden to provide a convincing line of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial burden is on the examiner to provide some suggestion of the desirability of doing what the inventor has done; either the references must expressly or impliedly suggest the claimed invention or the examiner must present a convincing line of reasoning as to why the artisan would have found the claimed invention obvious in light of the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Ex parte Clapp and MPEP §2144–§2144.09 for examples of adequate reasoning. The written rationale should be sufficient so that issues are clear and the applicant can respond; vague or conclusory assertions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all relied-on references in the rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a reference is relied on to support a rejection, whether or not in a minor capacity, that reference should be positively included in the statement of the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit references (even minor ones); include full citations and, where helpful, specific locations in the references. See In re Hoch for precedent. Including references ensures clarity and completeness of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of written record and explanation of rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important for an examiner to properly communicate the basis for a rejection so that the issues can be identified early and the applicant can be given fair opportunity to reply. The written record must clearly explain the rationale for decisions made during prosecution because issued patents are presumed valid and examiners cannot normally be compelled to testify about their mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit reasoning in the Office action; ensure the record is sufficient to support later interpretations of claim scope and to withstand litigation challenges (35 U.S.C. 282, 261).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date for patents and application publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the AIPA/2002 amendments (form paragraphs 7.12 / 7.12.01) to determine the 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of a U.S. patent or of a publication of a U.S. application, considering whether the reference was filed under 35 U.S.C. 111(a) or is a U.S. patent issued from, or a U.S./WIPO publication of, an international application with an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider priority/benefit claims to earlier-filed U.S. provisional applications (35 U.S.C. 119(e)), U.S. nonprovisional applications (35 U.S.C. 120 or 121), and international applications (35 U.S.C. 120, 121 or 365(c)) only if the relied-upon earlier-filed application's disclosure appropriately supports the subject matter. Do NOT consider priority/benefit claims to U.S. applications filed before an international application with international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000. Do NOT consider foreign priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 365(a). If an international application had an international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000 and did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English by WIPO, it is not prior art under 102(e) but may be applied under 102(a) or (b) as of its publication date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (or non-use) of patent application publications as 102(e) references
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent application publications may only be used as 102(e) references in specified circumstances (see form paragraphs 7.12/7.12.01); certain international publications filed before cut-off dates or not designating the U.S./not in English are not 102(e) references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a publication of an international application has an international filing date prior to November 29, 2000 and did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English by WIPO, do NOT use 102(e) form paragraph; treat the reference as potential 102(a) or 102(b) prior art as of publication date. See MPEP §§7.08–7.09, 7.12, 7.12.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 (when to make)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two applications of different inventive entities are copending (not published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)) and filing dates differ, a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 should be made in the later-filed application if the applications have a common assignee or a common inventor, unless the later application was filed on or after Nov 29, 1999 and the applications were commonly owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person at the time the later invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional rejections alert the applicant that an actual rejection can be expected if the earlier application issues; they preserve confidentiality of unpublished applications. See MPEP §706.02(k) and §706.02(l)(3) for procedure, and consider 35 U.S.C. 103(c) implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome provisional 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional rejection can be overcome by: (A) arguing patentability over the earlier filed application; (B) combining the subject matter of the copending applications into a single application claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of the prior applications and abandoning the copending applications (subject to 35 U.S.C. 112(first paragraph) support requirements); (C) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation (that unclaimed invention disclosed in the copending application was derived from the inventor of the other application); (D) filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 showing a date of invention prior to the effective U.S. filing date of the copending application; or (E) for applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, showing that the prior art and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, commonly owned or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that combining into a single application may not preserve 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit for claims that lack 112 support in prior applications; see Studiengesellschaft Kohle v. Shell Oil. Terminal disclaimers and 37 CFR procedures may also be relevant where common ownership exists and for double patenting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) disqualification of prior art (when prior art is excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another person which qualifies as prior art only under subsections (e), (f), and (g) of section 102 shall not preclude patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 103(c) applies only to obviousness determinations under 35 U.S.C. 103, not to whether subject matter qualifies as prior art under 102. If subject matter qualifies as prior art under any other subsection (e.g., 102(a), 102(b), or 102(e) for certain dates), it will not be disqualified by 103(c). The burden is on the applicant/patentee to establish common ownership at the relevant time. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing common ownership for 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be disqualified as prior art under 103(c), the subject matter and the claimed invention must have been commonly owned (wholly/100% owned) by the same person(s) or organization(s) at the time the claimed invention was made, or be subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person(s)/organization(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership requires full (100%) ownership of both the reference subject matter and the claimed invention by the same entity/entities at the relevant time. Ownership by different persons/organizations (or less than 100% ownership) defeats common ownership. A statement like “Application X and Patent Z were, at the time the invention of Application X was made, jointly owned by Companies A and B” may be sufficient evidence. Moral or unenforceable obligations do not establish common ownership. The burden of proof lies with the person asserting exclusion. See examples and MPEP §706.02(l)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and scope of 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: 103(c) applies only to prior art usable in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 and does not affect subject matter that qualifies as anticipatory prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 (including some 102(e) situations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if subject matter is disqualified under 103(c) for obviousness, non-statutory and statutory double patenting rejections based on such subject matter may still be appropriate. The examiner should place the burden of establishing disqualification on the applicant once a prima facie case of obviousness is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a continuing application to claim benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: An application claiming benefit of a prior-filed copending national or international application under 35 U.S.C. 120 must name as an inventor at least one inventor named in the prior filed application, and the prior filed application must disclose the named inventor’s invention claimed in at least one claim of the later-filed application in the manner provided by the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So long as at least one inventor is in common and other 120 requirements are met, the Office will permit a claim for 120 benefit without additional submissions unless examination reveals a need (e.g., intervening reference). Examiner should examine the earlier filed application to determine common inventorship and satisfaction of 112 support for at least one claim of the later application.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) public use or on-sale rejections (evidence requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) based upon a public use or sale of the invention requires that a full explanation of the evidence establishing a public use or sale be provided in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the Office action (bracket 2) includes a complete explanation of the supporting evidence and precede this form paragraph with the appropriate other form paragraphs as instructed (e.g., 7.07, 7.09, or 7.103).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(c) abandonment rejections (evidence requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) because the invention has been abandoned requires insertion of a full explanation of the evidence establishing abandonment of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed factual support and refer to MPEP §2134 for further guidance. Precede with proper form paragraphs as instructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) foreign patenting rejections (explanation requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(d) as being barred by foreign patenting requires an explanation which must include appropriate dates and how they make the foreign patent available under 35 U.S.C. 102(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert detailed dates and facts in the Office action (bracket 3) and refer to MPEP §2135 for applicable prior art; precede with proper form paragraphs as instructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(f) applicant not inventor (evidence requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) because the applicant did not invent the claimed subject matter requires an explanation of the supporting evidence establishing that applicant was not the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide supporting evidence and cite MPEP §2137 for required procedures; precede with required form paragraphs (e.g., 7.07 and 7.13 or 7.103).
